title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Medical equipment cleaning (external only)
audience: Owners of businesses that clean the external surfaces of medical equipment and furniture in clinics and care settings, who set per-batch prices or plan monthly revenue.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of an external equipment cleaning business as fixed or variable, including PPE, consumables and equipment upkeep
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level the business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. For an external equipment cleaner, the figure helps decide whether a new clinic contract or a second crew can pay for itself. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages behind it. The research found no medical-equipment cost or margin data, so every figure in this lesson is hypothetical and must be replaced with your own records.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of batches in a month. For this course they include insurance, phone and software, vehicle registration, loan repayments, the equipment you carry for external work, and training courses. Variable costs move with each batch. They include the cleaning products used on a batch, PPE used on a batch, the payment fees on each sale and any subcontractor fees. Work on reprocessing or internal devices is outside this course and carries no cost line here. ANZ defines fixed and variable costs and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss (21 February 2025). Express variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check that percentage across at least three periods.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. One minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales left to cover fixed costs. Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 18 per cent becomes 0.18 and the contribution margin is 0.82. Xero's glossary describes the same approach, dividing fixed costs by the contribution ratio and rounding a job count up to whole jobs (Xero, 23 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source, period and date. Then compute the contribution margin. Then divide the fixed costs by it to get break-even revenue. Divide that by your average batch price and round up to whole batches, because a part batch does not cover costs on its own. The sample plan that the base lesson draws on uses US figures from 2002, so none of its figures is used here. The method is the check: if you cannot source each input, do not use the result.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, check that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one, that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost, and that the output is revenue and not profit. Write down the reconciled figure with its inputs, and drop the others. Do not copy an equipment-cleaning break-even figure from another plan or a vendor page without its inputs.

procedure: List every monthly cost for the external equipment work and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average batch price, and round up to whole batches.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: Hypothetical figures, invented for this lesson and not medical-equipment data. A two-person external equipment cleaning business has fixed costs of $2,400 AUD a month, variable costs of 18 per cent of sales and an average batch price of $300 AUD.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many batches must the business complete each month to break even, and what should it check before setting prices?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.18, which is 0.82. Break-even revenue is $2,400 AUD divided by 0.82, which is $2,926.83 AUD a month. At $300 AUD a batch, that is 9.76 batches, so the business needs 10 batches to cover its costs. Each batch contributes $246.00 AUD ($300 AUD multiplied by 0.82) towards fixed costs. Before setting prices, check that the 18 per cent includes every cost of a batch, including PPE, that the $2,400 AUD is a monthly figure, and that $300 AUD is the average price actually charged after any discount.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months, with the period and source of each cost

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a plan without its inputs
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant.
No medical-equipment cost, price or margin source was found in the research for this course. Every figure in this lesson is hypothetical and must be replaced with your own records.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs. Do not copy another plan's break-even figure.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $2,400 AUD a month and variable costs are 18 per cent of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the client today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel
